reason_for_coming.note: The relationship is documented - 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord' - and the motive is this record's reading of a man arriving where his brother already was. Chain migration is the commonest reason anyone moved anywhere in this decade and it is almost never written down.

kin.note: ANDREAS NAMES THE BROTHERS IN ONE BREATH: 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord, came in 1831, and run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern' (History of Chicago vol. 1, the 1833 roster). The RELATIONSHIP is documented and this row does not doubt it. INFERRED, AND THE REASON IS THE IDENTIFICATION RATHER THAN THE TIE. Andreas prints the brother as 'Samuel, the landlord' and never with a surname; the town holds exactly one Samuel Miller — hh_miller_samuel, rung G1b, named by the 1832 muster, the Democrat and the 1833 tax list — and what ties him to Andreas's landlord is a shared surname carried by the sentence and the same three years in the same town. That is one agreement, and the crosswalk rule this project uses for a MERGE asks for a second. The trade does not supply it: hh_miller_samuel records no occupation, which is an absence rather than a disagreement, and this project's own miller_house record has the tavern 'past its innkeeping days' by the scene date. So the row is written at the grade the weakest link deserves. JOHN MILLER'S CARD SAYS SAMUEL 'is not written as a household here': that was true of the hand-authored parcel and stopped being true when the civic mint gave Samuel a card of his own, which is the card this row points at.

persons.note: ELECTED ONE OF THE FIVE FIRST TRUSTEES OF THE TOWN on 10 August 1833 with 20 of 28 votes, and Andreas notes that he 'being a candidate himself, refrained from voting' - so he is one of only two men in this parcel whose conduct at the poll is recorded. His brother Samuel Miller kept the tavern on the north bank at the forks and is not written as a household here, because Andreas's 1833 roster names him only in passing as 'Samuel, the landlord' and this project's miller_house record has the house 'past its innkeeping days' by the scene date. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. A YEAR off it is documented; a MONTH is not, and neither is anything about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Miller, John” (poll_1833_020, line 41); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Miller, John” (tax_1833_074, line 126); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Miller, John” (poll_1834_072, line 241). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Miller' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “John Miller” as fire warden (f1839_r0033, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Miller' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PARTNER IN THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST MANUFACTORY. Andreas: 'The only manufactory established at that early day was the rude shed called a tannery, near the Miller tavern, where John Miller and Benjamin Hall were tanning a few hides into a rough but endurable leather.' He signed the 1832 militia agreement. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “B. F. Hall” (f1839_v0626, printed page 45, ward 6, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Hall' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins B. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. research_note: THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST FACTORY AND ITS TWO NAMED WORKMEN, in a household assembled from three passages - the roster, Bates's 1883 interview and Andreas's own summary of the settlement's industry. A TANNERY IS A POPULATION FACT AS WELL AS A BUILDING: it takes hides from the butchers (Archibald Clybourne has his own household here) and it supplies the saddlers at Lake and Canal (Goss & Cobb, also here), so three of this parcel's households are one supply chain. That is the sort of structure the inferred phase should be looking for when it decides which trades the town must have had.

Names, places * , dates, and ages at death
of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well - known citizens who arrived after 1843, together
with others prominently connected with Illinois history:
old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. miller_john, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1031 (a single entry).
